correctness.rationale: The Pauli Bloch system is derived explicitly and recovers the exact commuting and no-hopping axes. Its second derivative gives strict early-time improvement. A positive symmetric part for N=M+2gamma I and nonvanishing first coordinate of all eigenvectors when ab is nonzero place every N eigenvalue in the open right half-plane; exponential-polynomial asymptotics then force unbounded rescaled measured distance. The Laplace resolvent and implicit simple pole at zero yield the quadratic eigenvalue and positive residue, with other poles faster. Exact rational characteristic and resolvent checks plus a Taylor-certified finite witness independently test calculations; these finite checks are not used to deduce universal claims.

originality.rationale: The 2026 permutation-group study proves the commuting/central-Hamiltonian all-time comparison and the two-state cosine formula, but explicitly excludes generic noncommuting Hamiltonians from its guarantee. The new result classifies the complete constant on-site detuning perturbation for two states and gives the precise slow-mode eigenvalue and population residue. The most relevant open-access graph-decoherence study uses a different noise channel and a fidelity-based quantum/classical map comparison. The searches and source inspections found no statement implying this exact iff, late-time-ratio and quadratic-residue combination. This is qualified best-knowledge originality, not certified priority.

A broader study of tilted bit-flip Lindblad qubits might have classified the same total-variation-to-uniform benchmark using different terminology.
A full inspection of every related controlled-qubit and general QSW source was not feasible; no global priority certification is claimed.

value.rationale: The result pinpoints the exact robustness boundary of a recent mathematically motivated quantum-assisted mixing inequality under the physically natural addition of on-site energy disorder. The global time quantifier and singular quadratic slow mode show that small noncommuting detuning can reverse the all-times comparison despite strict early-time gains. This is useful for interpreting noisy two-state devices and deciding which constant Hamiltonian perturbations preserve a uniform mixing guarantee. The two-state scope is explicitly limited; no generic multi-site theorem or improved first-hitting time is claimed.
